title: Pachomius' community
hook: monks living together under a rule: work, prayer, shared bread

segments.voice: Yesterday, Egeria's diary, pilgrimage, and your line was walk where they walked. What one detail did you write down for someone who wasn't there? Day seven hundred seventy-two.

Locked up with other recruits in a city on the Nile, rounded up for the emperor's army, sits a young man who isn't a Christian. He's hungry and far from home. And in the evening, strangers come with food and drink for the prisoners. He asks who they are. Christians, he's told: people who are kind to strangers, for the sake of the God of heaven. His name is Pachomius. The Life written about him says that night he promised that, if he got free, he would spend his life serving others. A few days ago we met Antony, who walked out alone into the desert. Pachomius goes into the desert too. But he doesn't stay alone.

After his release, Pachomius is baptized and learns the hard life of a hermit from an old monk. Then, at a deserted village by the river called Tabennesi, the story goes, he's told to build a place where many could live together. So he does. Then it gets hard. The Life says his first followers took advantage of him. He served them, cooked for them, did the chores, and they treated him like the help. Eventually he gave them a rule, and when they wouldn't keep it, he sent them away. Living together turned out to be harder than living alone. So Pachomius organized it. Monks lived in houses, each with a leader. They worked with their hands, weaving mats and baskets, and the work supported the community and the poor. They gathered to pray at set times. They ate together, the same food, at a shared table. The sick were cared for. Nobody owned anything privately. People kept coming, and more communities were founded along the river. The book of Acts had already described this way of life, in the first Christians in Jerusalem: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." The Greek word behind fellowship there is koinonia, a sharing, a life held in common. And Pachomius' communities came to be called by that same name: the Koinonia. Here's the idea at its plainest. Alone in a cave, nobody leaves dishes in your sink. Nobody snores. Nobody needs you when you're tired. In community, everyone does. As the Life tells it, for Pachomius that was the point.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you share space or work with: a household, roommates, a team, a congregation. Notice the small friction points. The dishes. The trash. The one who's always late, or the one who always has to fix things. Don't stew. Just notice. Now pick one chore that usually falls to one person, and imagine doing it alongside them, not instead of them. Folding the laundry together. Clearing the table side by side. Pachomius' monks shared the work and the bread. If you pray, you can pray for the people you live with, by name. The bell holds the time.
Pachomius' community. The shared life Pachomius built by the Nile: houses of monks under a rule, with work, prayer and bread held in common.
Your line: together is harder, and better. Today, share one chore with someone, side by side, and stay until it's done. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Christian monks and nuns in Orthodox, Catholic and other traditions live in community under a rule, sharing work, prayer at set hours, and meals.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing, a life in common. the word in Acts 2:42, and the name of Pachomius' communities.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks are people who get away from other people.
what it means: Pachomius gathered monks to live together, sharing work, prayer and bread under a rule.
what a scholar hears: the Koinonia, known through the Lives of Pachomius in Coptic and Greek, and his rule.

notes: Conscription story: Christians bring food to the recruits; he is told they are kind to strangers for the God of heaven; he promises to serve. Paraphrased from the Life; confirm details and city (Thebes in some versions).
His training under the hermit Palamon and the call at Tabennesi ('the story goes') are paraphrased; confirm.
The first followers who took advantage of him and were sent away: confirm in the Bohairic Life.
Description of houses with leaders, mat and basket weaving, common prayer, common meals, care for the sick, no private property: confirm against the Rule.
'People kept coming, and more communities were founded along the river' avoids numbers; confirm.
The Pachomian federation is called the Koinonia in the sources; confirm. Original: κοινωνία, pronunciation given in a Koine-friendly form; modern Greek is kee-no-NEE-a.
howItsDone names Orthodox and Catholic monastic life; confirm wording.
